title: The Kellogg Brothers Fall Out over Corn Flakes
text:
John Harvey Kellogg was a famous doctor who ran the Battle Creek Sanitarium in Michigan, a health resort that promoted vegetarian food, exercise and abstinence. His younger brother, Will Keith Kellogg, worked for him for about twenty-five years as bookkeeper, manager and general helper, for modest pay and little recognition.

In the 1890s, while looking for digestible foods for the patients, the brothers developed a process for making flakes from boiled wheat, and later from corn. The flakes were a success with patients, and Will saw that they could be sold to the whole country. John was not interested in mass marketing, and he objected to Will's plan to add sugar, which he considered unhealthy.

In 1906 Will struck out on his own and founded the company that became Kellogg's, putting his signature on every box. The brothers then fought for years in court over who had the right to use the family name on cereal. Will won.

They never truly reconciled. According to family accounts and later biographers, near the end of his life John wrote his brother a long letter of apology, but it was held back by a secretary and Will did not see it until after John's death in 1943. Will, by then nearly blind, had given most of his fortune to the W. K. Kellogg Foundation, devoted to children's health and education.
lesson: Brothers who cannot agree on a shared enterprise may lose each other along with it. Say what needs saying while the other person can still hear it.
people: John Harvey Kellogg, Will Keith Kellogg
source: Howard Markel, The Kelloggs: The Battling Brothers of Battle Creek (2017)
caveat: The story of the undelivered letter comes from family accounts and is not fully documented.
